summary: Explains that TCP connections are vulnerable to forged reset (RST) packets, especially between well-known endpoints on predictable ports, such as BGP sessions. It discusses ways to make such attacks harder and the tradeoffs involved. It is informational guidance, not a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP accepts a reset packet when its sequence number fits the connection's receive window. RFC 4953 explains how attackers can guess that number and compares ways to make forged resets harder.

subtitle: Why forged TCP reset packets can disrupt long-lived connections and how defenses compare

tldr.problem: An off-path attacker may forge a TCP reset for a connection with known endpoints and ports, especially when its receive window is large.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4953 analyzes how guessing a sequence number can reset a connection and reviews transport-, network-, and ICMP-level defenses.
tldr.outcome: The Informational survey defines no new protocol. It explains trade-offs among authentication, address filtering, and stricter TCP reset checks.

today: RFC 4953 is an Informational survey published in July 2007. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it defines no new standard.

sections.title: How a Forged Reset Can Work
sections.content:
A TCP reset (RST) terminates a connection. An off-path attacker who cannot see the connection may still send a forged RST if the attacker knows the endpoint addresses and ports and guesses a sequence number accepted by the receiver.

The RFC focuses on long-lived connections between known endpoints, including BGP sessions. A router that loses a BGP connection may treat its peer as unreachable and remove routes, increasing the impact of a reset.
sections.plainLanguage: A forged reset can make a TCP connection stop. If a router treats a lost BGP connection as a routing failure, the effect can spread beyond that connection.

sections.title: Why Larger Receive Windows Increase Risk
sections.content:
TCP accepts a reset when its sequence number falls inside the current receive window. For a small window under the assumptions in the RFC, a blind guess has odds of 1 in 57,000.

High-bandwidth paths often need larger receive windows to keep data moving. The attacker can also send guesses faster on a faster path, so RFC 4953 says exposure can grow with the square of bandwidth. Its estimates assume the attacker knows the connection's addresses and ports.
sections.plainLanguage: A larger receive window gives an attacker more sequence numbers that TCP may accept. Faster networks also let the attacker send more guesses in less time.

sections.title: Transport-Level Defenses
sections.content:
TCP MD5 authenticates each segment, including resets, using a shared key. The RFC notes that key setup and processing cost can make this difficult to use broadly.

Other proposals accept a reset only at a narrowly specified sequence number, check TCP timestamps, or reduce receive-window size. These approaches have trade-offs: some change TCP control behavior, timestamps may be guessed, and a smaller window can reduce throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport defenses add checks to TCP itself. Stronger checks can require shared keys or protocol changes, while smaller receive windows can limit connection speed.

sections.title: Network and ICMP Defenses
sections.content:
Address filtering can discard packets whose source address is implausible for where they entered a network. It works best when network borders apply it consistently; it does not provide a standalone defense for every pair of endpoints.

IPsec can authenticate packets across protocols, but requires suitable keys or certificates and can add processing and management costs. The RFC also discusses forged ICMP messages, which may affect TCP connections and require careful validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Network-level defenses can check packet sources before TCP processes them. Filtering depends on coordinated network borders, while IPsec needs key management.

sections.title: Limits and Overall Findings
sections.content:
Each defense addresses different threats. Clear-text checks, such as a sequence number learned from earlier traffic, may stop off-path attackers but do not protect against an attacker who can observe the connection. Cryptographic authentication can also resist on-path spoofing.

RFC 4953 concludes that no approach is free of costs. Transport checks must be added to each transport protocol, while network-layer defenses need coordination or key infrastructure. Application-layer security protects application data but cannot prevent a forged reset from disrupting TCP first.
sections.plainLanguage: No single defense fits every connection. A check that stops someone who cannot see the traffic may not stop someone who can observe it.
